procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and decree dated December 21, 1959 of the Allahabad High Court in First Appeal No. 87 of 1948.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The trial court's decree in favor of the plaintiff (idol) was upheld by the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The defendants appealed to the Supreme Court with a certificate challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the High Court that the suit was maintainable.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the suit filed by the idol represented by a worshipper, in the circumstances of the case, is maintainable.

facts: The manager (Shebait) of a temple alienated property belonging to the temple's idol.
A worshipper, who also assisted in the temple's management, filed a suit as the 'next friend' of the idol to challenge the alienation.
The suit sought a declaration that the property belonged to the idol and the recovery of its possession.

The defendants argued that the suit was not maintainable for two reasons: 1) it was barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and 2) only the Shebait, not a worshipper, could file a suit on behalf of the idol.
law: An idol is a juridical person, similar to a minor.
Ordinarily, only the Shebait (manager) can represent the idol in legal proceedings.

A suit is barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure only if it is for one of the specific reliefs enumerated in that section, such as removing a trustee or altering a trust scheme. A suit by an idol to enforce its private right to property (e.g., for title and possession) falls outside the scope of Section 92.

An exception to the general rule of representation exists: if the Shebait acts adversely to the idol's interests or fails to protect them, a worshipper has the right to represent the idol in a suit to protect its interests.
application: The Court first determined that Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not a bar to the suit. It reasoned that the suit was filed by the idol to enforce its private right to recover its property from someone in illegal possession. Since the reliefs sought (declaration of title and possession) are not among those listed in Section 92, the section did not apply.

The Court then addressed the main issue of whether a worshipper could represent the idol. It acknowledged the general rule that the Shebait is the proper representative. However, it held that an exception must be made when the Shebait acts against the idol's interests, as in this case where the Shebait himself had improperly alienated the property.

The Court reasoned that an idol is in the position of a minor. When its legal guardian (the Shebait) abandons it or acts improperly, an interested person, such as a worshipper, must be allowed to step in to protect the minor's interests. To require the worshipper to first file a separate, lengthy suit to remove the Shebait would be impractical and could cause irreparable harm to the idol.

Therefore, the Court concluded that in circumstances where the Shebait's actions are adverse to the idol, a worshipper can be clothed with an 'ad hoc' power of representation to file a suit and recover the idol's property.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the suit filed by the idol, represented by the worshipper, was maintainable. The Court reasoned that the suit was not barred by Section 92 of the CPC, and that a worshipper has the right to represent the idol to protect its property when the official manager (Shebait) is acting adversely to the idol's interests.

issue.issue_text: Whether the suit for a declaration of the idol's title to property and for possession of the same is barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

facts: A suit was filed on behalf of a Hindu idol.
The reliefs sought were a declaration that certain property belonged to the idol and the recovery of possession of that property from a person in alleged illegal possession.
law: For a suit to be barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, three conditions must be met: (1) it must concern a public trust, (2) there must be a breach of trust or a need for court direction, and (3) the relief claimed must be one of those specifically enumerated in Section 92.
A suit for a declaration of title to property and for possession of that property is not one of the reliefs enumerated in Section 92.
A suit by an idol, as a juristic person, to enforce its private right to recover its property from those who unlawfully interfere with it is not a suit to which Section 92 applies.
application: The Court analyzed the suit from two perspectives.

First, it characterized the suit as an action by the idol to enforce its private right to recover its property from someone in illegal possession. Such a suit for the enforcement of a private right falls outside the scope of Section 92.

Second, the Court examined the specific reliefs claimed. It noted that the suit was for a declaration of the idol's title and for possession of the property. Since these reliefs are not among those listed in Section 92, the third condition for the section's application was not met.
Because the suit could be seen as either enforcing a private right or seeking reliefs not covered by Section 92, it was outside the purview of that section.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the suit was not barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure because it was a suit by the idol to enforce its private right to property and because the reliefs sought (declaration of title and possession) are not among those enumerated in that section.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts that the impugned transaction was not binding on the idol and was not supported by consideration.

facts: The trial court and the High Court both held that the sale of the idol's property was not for the benefit of the deity and that the consideration was not adequate.
These are referred to as "concurrent findings" because both lower courts came to the same conclusion on these questions of fact.
law: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts, especially when those findings are based on an appreciation of the evidence presented.
application: The appellant's counsel attempted to argue against the correctness of the lower courts' findings of fact.
The Supreme Court stated that it would not be justified in allowing the appellant to question these findings.
The Court's reasoning was that the findings were concurrent and were based on an appreciation of the relevant evidence by the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court explicitly accepted the concurrent findings of the lower courts and refused to interfere with them. It therefore upheld the determination that the transaction was not binding on the idol and was not supported by consideration.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the suit filed by the idol represented by a worshipper, in the circumstances of the case, is maintainable.
appellant_arguments: Only the Shebait (manager) was entitled to file the suit and represent the deity, not a worshipper.
respondent_arguments: The suit filed on behalf of the idol by a worshipper, who also assisted in the temple's management, is maintainable to challenge the alienation of the idol's property.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the suit for a declaration of the idol's title to property and for possession of the same is barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
appellant_arguments: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure was a bar to the suit.
respondent_arguments: The suit for a declaration of title and recovery of possession is not barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts that the impugned transaction was not binding on the idol and was not supported by consideration.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court should interfere and question the correctness of the lower courts' concurrent findings of fact that the transaction was not binding on the idol and lacked consideration.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts as they are based on an appreciation of relevant evidence.

cases.principle: To support the court's finding that a suit filed by an idol, represented by a worshipper, is maintainable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A suit by an idol, as a juristic person represented by a worshipper, for a declaration of its title to property and for possession of the same from a third party is maintainable. Such a suit is for the enforcement of the idol's private rights and falls outside the scope of Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the reliefs of declaration and possession are not among those enumerated in that section.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A suit filed by a worshipper on behalf of an idol to declare the idol's title to property and recover possession from a person holding it under a void alienation is maintainable. Such a suit is not barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure because it is a suit to enforce the idol's private right to its property, and the reliefs of declaration of title and possession are not among those enumerated in that section.
legal_tests_applied: To invoke Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, three conditions must be satisfied: (i) the trust is created for public purposes of a charitable or religious nature; (ii) there was a breach of trust or a direction of court is necessary in the administration of such a trust; and (iii) the relief claimed is one or other of the reliefs enumerated therein. If any of the three conditions is not satisfied, the suit falls outside the scope of the said section.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that only a Shebait could file the suit was rejected because Privy Council decisions are authorities for the position that apart from a Shebait, under certain circumstances, the idol can be represented by disinterested persons like a worshipper.

The argument that Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure barred the suit failed because the suit was filed by the idol to enforce its private right to possession of its property from a person in illegal possession. The reliefs sought—a declaration of title and possession—are not among the reliefs enumerated in Section 92.
why_respondent_won: The suit filed by the idol represented by a worshipper was held to be maintainable, as numerous decisions have permitted a worshipper in such circumstances to represent the idol and to recover property for the idol.

The suit was found to be outside the purview of Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure because it was for a declaration of the idol's title and for possession of its property, which is a suit to enforce a private right, not a suit for one of the reliefs concerning the administration of a public trust mentioned in that section.
policy_considerations: If worshippers were not allowed to file a suit on behalf of the idol and had to first file a suit for the removal of a Shebait and the appointment of another, such a procedure would be prolonged and complicated, and the interest of the idol might irreparably suffer. Allowing a worshipper to sue directly protects the idol's interests more effectively.
